name: CoPS: Empowering LLM Agents with Provable Cross-Task Experience Sharing
venue: ICLR 2025 (Poster). Listed as 'ICLR 2025 Poster' in the OpenReview ICLR.cc/2025/Conference submissions (Submission #12611, forum id=9W6Z9IeLzc). An earlier version was also a poster at the NeurIPS 2024 Language Gamification Workshop (LanGame, forum id=8DLW1saLEY, Submission #18). Preprint arXiv:2410.16670 (cs.LG; cs.AI), submitted 22 Oct 2024 (v1).
authors_affiliation: Chen Yang (Indiana University Bloomington), Chenyang Zhao* (University of California, Los Angeles), Quanquan Gu (University of California, Los Angeles; co-corresponding), Dongruo Zhou (Indiana University Bloomington; co-corresponding). *Equal contribution (Chen Yang and Chenyang Zhao). Two institutions: Department of Computer Science, Indiana University Bloomington and Department of Computer Science, UCLA.
task_domain: LLM-agent sequential reasoning / interactive decision-making across embodied household tasks (ALFWorld), web shopping (WebShop), and multi-hop knowledge-intensive QA (HotPotQA). Spans embodied, web, and QA agent domains.
problem_setting: Interactive, single-agent gradient-free sequential decision-making formalized as a task space M, state space S, action space A where state s is a text history and an experience tau is a complete trial (success reward r=1, else 0). The agent solves each task over up to 10 trials with cross-trial and cross-task experience sharing. CoPS is designed to work in two settings: (1) OFFLINE, where the agent has access to an external static dataset/memory bank of pre-collected experiences (possibly from other tasks/agents); and (2) ONLINE, where the agent gathers its own experiences through environment interaction and appends them to the memory bank after each trial. No parameter updates (pure in-context). Supervision is the binary environment success signal r(tau). A theoretical framework analyzes OfflineCoPS (pessimism principle) and OnlineCoPS (optimism principle) with provable suboptimality / regret bounds depending on LLM pretraining quality and distribution matching.
what_is_retrieved: Past experiences = complete prior-task trial trajectories (tau, full text trials) from a memory bank. Successful cross-task experience trajectories are selected and concatenated as in-context demonstrations. The retrievable unit is the whole trial trajectory; the method explicitly supports experiences from DIFFERENT tasks than the current one (cross-task sharing).
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID by design / GROWING in the main experiments. The memory bank D may be a static external pre-collected dataset (offline setting) OR a self-grown episodic store the agent writes to after each trial (online setting). In the reported Alfworld/Webshop/HotPotQA experiments the bank is grown online over 10 trials per task (and shared across tasks), so it functions as a growing/episodic memory; the offline variant treats it as a static corpus. No external KB/doc corpus is retrieved.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Distribution-matching / fixed-size sampling objective rather than a deterministic top-k ranking or a completeness/minimal-set objective. CoPS solves p_hat = argmax_p E_{tau~p}[r(tau)] - d(p, Dec(.|s1)) (a pessimism-regularized reward-maximizing distribution over the bank), then samples k experiences i.i.d. from p_hat(tau) proportional to r(tau)*exp(-c*cos-distance). k is a fixed in-context memory size (k=5 in experiments; plateaus at k=3). It is a fixed-k selection but via stochastic distribution-matched sampling, not similarity argmax top-k (the c->infinity limit recovers nearest-neighbor; c=0 is uniform over successes).
retrieval_unit: full trajectory: a complete trial / experience tau (the full text of a prior task's trial, including the thought-action-observation sequence). Multiple selected trajectories tau^1..tau^k are concatenated into one experience collection T = tau^1 | ... | tau^k.
index_source: Growing memory (online setting, used in the headline experiments) or static external dataset (offline setting); hybrid construction. The bank D is unrestricted and may contain experiences for different tasks or different solution strategies for the same task. In the online experiments the bank is initialized and grown from the agent's own trials across tasks; the method also supports a pre-collected/external (e.g., from other agents or RL systems) static bank.
index_structure_topology: Flat store of trajectory experiences. Each experience is embedded with a language embedding model (gte-Qwen2 7B) into a Euclidean vector; selection scores experiences by cosine distance to a decoder-produced reference experience tau^{s1}. No graph, hierarchy, or cluster structure; it is a flat memory bank with embedding-based scoring.
retriever_type: Dense embedding-based selection (off-the-shelf gte-Qwen2 7B Instruct embeddings) combined with a reward-weighted, pessimism-regularized sampling distribution. Not BM25, not a learned/trained retriever, not LLM-as-retriever; the LLM itself supplies the 'decoder' reference experience but selection is embedding cosine + reward weighting.
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf embedder) plus reward weighting; the selection rule is theoretically derived (pessimism principle from offline RL), not trained. The embedding function e is a fixed pretrained model (gte-Qwen2 7B); the selection probability p_hat(tau) is proportional to the binary task reward r(tau) times exp(-c*cosine-distance to the decoder reference). There is no contrastive training, no LM-feedback fine-tuning, no RL-trained retriever; the only 'signal' is the binary success reward used as a multiplicative weight and the embedding similarity.
query_construction: Raw initial-state-conditioned reference. CoPS uses a 'decoder' (Dec) that, given the current initial state s1, outputs a reference experience tau^{s1} from the bank that starts with the same initial state s1 (most recent one if several) - reflecting how the LLM would solve the task without intervention. The query/key is therefore the embedding of this decoder reference experience tau^{s1} (an LLM-behavior proxy for the current task), not a hand-built query; experiences are scored by cosine distance to it.
query_granularity: task-level / trial-level (one-shot per trial at t=0). The decoder reference and the experience selection are computed once at the start of each trial from the initial state s1; the selected experience collection T is then fixed for the whole step-by-step rollout of that trial. (Contrasts with RAP, which re-retrieves per stage within a trial.)
when_to_retrieve: one-shot per trial. Selection is performed once at the beginning of each trial (each of the up to 10 trials per task triggers a fresh selection), then the concatenated experiences are kept fixed during the within-trial step-by-step action generation. No within-trial uncertainty-triggered or adaptive re-retrieval.
retrieval_trigger_signal: fixed schedule (per-trial). Selection is triggered unconditionally at the start of every trial; there is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-classifier/reflection-token trigger and no agent-initiated mid-trial retrieval. The paper highlights that because the prompt prefix is shared/fixed across trials, this enables prefix-caching efficiency (vs RAP's frequent per-stage embedding queries).
reranking: No separate reranking stage. Experiences are scored once by the reward-weighted exp(-c*cosine-distance) distribution p_hat and sampled; there is no cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranker. The scalar c interpolates between uniform sampling over successes (c=0) and deterministic nearest-experience selection (c->infinity).
retrieved_context_refinement: None / minimal. Selected successful experience trajectories tau^1..tau^k are concatenated verbatim into a single trajectory T and placed at the beginning of the prompt; no compression, decomposition, distillation, or distractor-filtering is applied. The reward-weighting (only successful, r=1, experiences receive positive probability) acts as an implicit relevance/quality filter at selection time rather than a post-retrieval refinement.
how_retrieved_used: prompt augmentation: the concatenated selected experience collection T = tau^1 | ... | tau^k is prepended to the prompt, and the agent then generates each action a_h ~ LLM(. | T, s_h) conditioned on T and the current state. No fine-tuning or latent-token injection; experiences are reused in-context as demonstrations of how to solve (cross-task) trials.
planning_integration: retrieve-then-plan, one-shot exemplars at trial start. Per trial, CoPS (1) selects k distribution-matched successful experiences via the pessimism objective, (2) concatenates them into T, then (3) runs the LLM agent step-by-step (a_h ~ LLM(.|T,s_h)) until success or the step budget H. No MCTS/tree search (explicitly contrasted with LATS's tree search), no hierarchical subtask decomposition, no per-step re-retrieval. Across trials, the online memory bank grows and the selection improves, giving cross-trial/cross-task improvement.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-trial / per-episode (per-answer at the trial level). Experience selection and prompt augmentation happen once per trial; within a trial the selected context is fixed while the agent emits a multi-step thought-action-observation rollout. Not per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call.
retrieved_item_representation: raw trajectory: selected experiences are injected as raw full prior trials (concatenated text trajectories of thought/action/observation steps) used as in-context demonstrations. No distillation into guidelines, no executable skills, no latent tokens.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: raw trajectory (concrete full prior-trial demonstrations). CoPS deliberately reuses successful raw experience trajectories as demonstrations rather than distilling them into higher-level strategies, insights, or workflows; its novelty is the principled distribution-matched SELECTION of these raw trajectories, not their abstraction.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Pessimism-based distribution matching: the selection objective penalizes distribution shift from the LLM's own decoder distribution (d(p, Dec(.|s1))), keeping selected experiences close to what the LLM would naturally do for the current task, which provably guards against risky out-of-distribution / poorly-matched experiences. Reward weighting restricts positive selection probability to successful (r=1) experiences. The scalar c tunes the adaptability-vs-robustness trade-off (smaller models benefit from a small nonzero c). Theoretically, the suboptimality/regret is bounded by the LLM pretraining error times a chi-square distribution-mismatch term, formalizing robustness to distribution shift.
memory_type: episodic experience bank (a memory bank D of full prior trials). Can be a self-grown online episodic store or an external static dataset; not a skill-library, workflow, graph, or latent memory.
write_back: Yes (in the online setting). After completing a trial, the agent appends the new experience trajectory to the memory bank D for future use (Algorithm 1, online line: 'the agent updates the memory bank D by adding the new experience'). In the offline setting the bank is a fixed pre-collected dataset (no write-back).
online_growth: Yes (online setting, used in the main Alfworld/Webshop/HotPotQA experiments): the bank grows trial-by-trial during deployment as new trials are added, enabling cross-trial improvement over the 10 trials and cross-task sharing. In the offline-setting variant the bank is static.
write_back_trigger: on-trial-completion (every finished trial is appended in the online setting), i.e., per-trial append regardless of success/failure outcome of that trial (the experience's reward r(tau) is stored alongside and used to weight future selection). It is not reflective/critique-gated and not human-validated; storage happens automatically at the end of each trial. (Offline: never / no write-back.)
failure_experience_usage: Failures are stored (every trial, including failed ones with r=0, is appended to the online bank) but are effectively NOT reused for prompting: the selection probability p_hat(tau) is proportional to the reward r(tau), so r=0 (failed) experiences get zero selection probability and only successful experiences are surfaced as demonstrations. So failures are recorded but not used as negative/contrastive demonstrations; no failure-derived corrective rules. Baselines like Reflexion/LATS instead reflect on failures.
memory_evolution_update: append-only. New trial experiences (with their rewards) are added to D; stored experiences are not merged, deduplicated, refined, overwritten, or pruned in the method (the decoder simply prefers the most-recent same-initial-state experience). The Limitations section notes that outdated/poorly-aligned experiences can hurt and suggests dynamic memory management as future work, implying no automatic forgetting/pruning.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Partly principled-but-not-learned: experience selection IS a theoretically optimized SELECTION POLICY (the pessimism/optimism-principled distribution p_hat over the bank derived from offline/online RL theory with provable suboptimality/regret), but it is NOT a trained/RL-updated parametric policy and NOT a fixed similarity top-k either. It is a closed-form reward-weighted, distribution-matched sampling rule (r(tau)*exp(-c*cosine)) with theoretical guarantees, sitting between fixed top-k and learned RL retrieval.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Cross-TASK sharing within a single agent is the central contribution: experiences from previously solved (different) tasks are shared and selected for new tasks. The offline setting also allows ingesting experiences from EXTERNAL sources (e.g., other agents / RL systems / pre-collected datasets), enabling a form of cross-source experience sharing, but the method is single-agent and does not implement collaborative multi-agent or cross-framework memory sharing (multi-agent extension is listed as future work).
benchmarks: ALFWorld (134 tasks, simulated household, textual feedback), WebShop (50 products, catalog of >1M items, HTML page + search engine interaction), and HotPotQA (100 multi-hop QA tasks, Wikipedia retrieval). Each algorithm is evaluated over up to 10 trials per task.
baselines: Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2024, reflection-driven multi-trial self-improvement, up to 3 recent same-task reflections), RAP (Kagaya et al. 2024, retrieval-augmented planning with per-stage top-k trajectory-fragment in-context demonstrations), and LATS (Zhou et al. 2023, Language Agent Tree Search, tree-structured search with reflection). React is cited as the underlying ICL agent foundation but is not a main results baseline.
key_metrics: Task success rate (%) - success after up to 10 trials (ALFWorld over 134 tasks, WebShop over 50 products x10 trials each, HotPotQA over 100 QA tasks). Sample-efficiency metric: total number of generated tokens (Table 3, WebShop) as a compute/efficiency proxy.
headline_result: CoPS consistently outperforms SOTA baselines across all three benchmarks and both model sizes. ALFWorld: 94% (Llama 3.1 8B) and 100% (70B), vs Reflexion 86%/94% and RAP 70%/93% - notably CoPS with the small 8B model (94%) matches Reflexion's 70B (94%). WebShop: 50% (8B) / 56% (70B), vs RAP 42%/42% (best baseline), a +8% (8B) and +14% (70B) absolute gain; Reflexion 30%/30%, LATS 24%/32%. HotPotQA: 63% (8B) / 65% (70B), vs Reflexion 56%/61% and LATS 55%/64%. Efficiency: on WebShop with Llama 3.1 8B, LATS generates 1,555,365 tokens vs CoPS 314,336 (>=5x fewer), under matched runtime.
ablations: Two hyperparameters ablated on ALFWorld (Llama 3.1 8B and 70B): (1) Scaling factor c in {0,1,5,10} with k=5 fixed - for the smaller 8B model a small nonzero c (e.g., c=1) generally yields the best performance, balancing adaptability vs robustness; larger models are less sensitive. This empirically matches Theorem 5.4's insight that more powerful LLMs should align more strongly with the decoder distribution. (2) Number of in-context experiences k from 1 to 10 with c=0 - performance improves up to k=3 then plateaus for both model sizes, so >3 experiences give minimal gains. Final hyperparameters (Table 5): ALFWorld k=5,c=5 (both sizes); WebShop k=5,c=0; HotPotQA k=5,c=5 (8B) and k=5,c=0 (70B).
evaluation_decoupling: No. Only end-to-end task success rate (and token-count efficiency) is reported; no intrinsic retrieval/selection metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, selection completeness) are reported separately - selection quality is evaluated indirectly through downstream success and the theoretical suboptimality/regret bounds.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Primarily outcome (binary task success rate, r(tau) in {0,1}). A sample-efficiency / process-cost proxy is reported (total generated tokens, Table 3) and trends over the 10 trials are shown (Figure: success rate vs trial index). No step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality metric. Theoretical guarantees (suboptimality gap, regret) provide a process-level analysis but are not empirical metrics.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Strong efficiency emphasis. On WebShop, CoPS generates far fewer tokens than tree-search LATS (8B: 314,336 vs 1,555,365, ~5x; 70B: 113,849 vs 1,058,752, ~9x) under matched runtime, and the fixed shared prompt prefix across trials maximizes prefix-caching in modern LLM-serving (SGLang), giving efficiency gains over RAP's frequent per-stage embedding queries. CoPS also achieves higher accuracy with the smaller 8B model than baselines need 70B for (ALFWorld 94% 8B = Reflexion 70B), i.e., better accuracy-per-compute. No dollar/latency figures, but token counts and serving-efficiency arguments are central. Token counts for Reflexion/RAP on WebShop are also tabulated (8B: 159,131 / 107,504; 70B: 125,406 / 109,245).
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed-k selection, budget-capped by k. In experiments k=5 in-context experiences per trial (Table 5), though the ablation shows performance plateaus at k=3. Selection is reward-weighted distribution-matched sampling of k trajectories (proportional to r(tau)*exp(-c*cosine)) rather than reranked-then-truncated; the scalar c (in {0,5} across benchmarks) controls how peaked the selection distribution is. The selected experiences are concatenated and prepended; prompt budget is bounded by k trajectories.
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (uses existing benchmarks: ALFWorld 134 tasks; WebShop 50 products evaluated x 10 trials; HotPotQA 100 QA tasks; up to 10 trials per task).
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: yes (distribution-matched, pessimism-based selection of prior-task experience trajectories from the memory bank), Reuse: yes (concatenated raw experiences used as in-context demonstrations for the new task), Revise: no (retrieved trajectories are used verbatim and not adapted/edited per case at solve time), Retain: yes in the online setting (new trial experiences appended to the memory bank); no in the offline setting].
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The paper frames itself as cross-task experience sharing / experience-assisted sequential reasoning grounded in offline-RL pessimism and online-learning optimism principles (citing Jin et al. 2021 pessimism, Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2011 optimism, Lin et al. 2023 in-context RL theory). It does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not use the term 'case-based reasoning'; it realizes Retrieve/Reuse/Retain mechanisms under an experience-sharing / RAG-for-decision-making framing.
tool_document_engineering: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; tools/environments are fixed per benchmark - ALFWorld actions, WebShop search/HTML, HotPotQA Wikipedia search).
index_content_separation: N/A. No separation of a lightweight index from heavy content; experiences are embedded for scoring and the full selected trajectories are loaded into the prompt.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A (not a tool-retrieval system; no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling tool index; environment interaction is via each benchmark's native action interface).
adaptation_mechanism: Verbatim ICL exemplar reuse: selected experience trajectories are concatenated and injected as-is as in-context demonstrations; there is no explicit case adaptation/revision, execution-feedback rewriting, critic-guided revision, or fine-tuning of the retrieved cases. Adaptation to the current task happens implicitly through the LLM conditioning on T plus the principled distribution-matched selection that picks experiences closest to the current task's decoder distribution.
builds_on: React (Yao et al. 2022b, ICL agent foundation); RAP (Kagaya et al. 2024, retrieval of in-context demonstrations for agents - CoPS adds principled selection and avoids per-stage manual splitting); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2024); LATS (Zhou et al. 2023); pessimism principle in offline RL (Jin et al. 2021); optimism principle in online decision-making (Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2011); in-context RL / LLM-agent statistical theory (Lin et al. 2023; He et al. 2024; Park et al. 2024 on regret of LLM agents); Raparthy et al. 2023 (high-quality experiences as ICL demonstrations from external RL systems); gte-Qwen2 embeddings (Li et al. 2023b); SGLang serving with prefix caching (Zheng et al. 2023); Llama 3.1 (Dubey et al. 2024).
contrasts_with: Reflection-driven reasoning (Reflexion, LATS) that relies only on pretrained-model knowledge and same-task self-reflection, limiting novel-scenario performance and risking hallucination; experience-assisted reasoning that depends on manually-curated or external-expert experiences and lacks clear principles for selecting representative examples (RAP - which also needs frequent per-stage embedding queries and benchmark-specific manual trajectory splitting, and lacks an effective selection algorithm); resource-intensive tree-search methods (LATS) with poor sample efficiency; fine-tuning-based agent learning (Feng et al. 2024) with high compute cost. CoPS instead offers a single, theoretically grounded, benchmark-agnostic, distribution-matched cross-task selection rule.
lineage: Group D (case-based / experience planning): a theory-grounded experience-selection LLM agent in the lineage of retrieval-augmented / experience-assisted planners (React -> Reflexion / RAP -> CoPS). It advances the sub-topic by providing a provable pessimism-based (offline) / optimism-based (online) experience-selection policy with suboptimality and regret bounds, distinguishing it from heuristic similarity-top-k experience retrieval (RAP) and from insight-distillation experience agents (e.g., ExpeL).
